| [LIT-096](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-096.md) | What Is It Like to Be a Bat? | Nagel (1974), [DOI-10.2307/2183914](https://doi.org/10.2307/2183914). An organism has conscious states if and only if there is something it is like to be that organism. That subjective character belongs to a type of point of view, and it is left out by every functional, intentional or causal analysis, since each is compatible with its absence. Reduction elsewhere moves away from a point of view toward the objective; here that move leads away from the thing being explained. So physicalism may be true, but we have no conception of how it could be. Nagel proposes an "objective phenomenology" that would describe experience to beings who cannot have it. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 (NOTE-089); the source of the "something it is like" criterion of consciousness that the record's AI-consciousness work (LIT-056) adopts as its target, and of the argument that no functional analysis can settle whether that criterion is met. |

Veit's reply to five commentaries on *A Philosophy for the Science of Animal Consciousness* (2023). Its main new content is the metaphysics the book left to one paragraph. | [LIT-143](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-143.md) v2 | What is a Mathematical Structure of Conscious Experience? | Kleiner & Ludwig (2023), [ARXIV-2301.11812](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.11812). The paper proposes a definition, (MSC). A mathematical structure S = ((A_i), (S_j)) is a structure *of* conscious experience iff (S1) its domains are sets of experiential aspects, and (S2) every relation or function S_j has an "S_j-aspect". An S_j-aspect is an aspect that a variation of experience changes exactly when the variation fails to preserve S_j. The older condition (MDC), that a structure is "of" experience if its domains are aspects and its axioms hold, survives only as the necessary condition for *describing* experience, because as a sufficient condition it admits incompatible structures (discrete and non-discrete topologies on the same set), arbitrary re-definitions (every C·d for C > 0) and consciousness-indifferent structures. Worked examples: experienced relative similarity is a strict partial order that satisfies (MSC), given transitivity (assumed). Visual regions form a topology that satisfies (MSC), given Bayne and Chalmers's subsumptive unity thesis. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 (NOTE-135); worth reading as the most explicit criterion for when a formal model is *of* experience rather than a convenient description of it. Its two positive results are conditional: transitivity of relative similarity is assumed, and the topology result assumes the subsumptive unity thesis. Cite the Synthese version, which has dropped v1's argument against metric structure. |
| [LIT-146](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-146.md) v2 | The Moral Status of Animals | Gruen & Monsó (2003), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/moral-animal/>. The entry reviews five proposed grounds of moral considerability (species membership, human-exceptional capacities, personhood, sentience and agency). Its conclusion is that attempts to establish human uniqueness by capacities are "not the most promising" (§1.2). It then separates *having* moral status from the *weight* of a claim ("showing up on a moral radar screen", §2.2). Weight depends on the value theory adopted for animal interests (hedonism, preference satisfaction, objective list; §2.1) and on the normative framework (rights, which are absolute but generate forward-looking duties when violated, or a multi-factor utilitarianism). It closes with virtue-ethical, feminist, relational and empathy-based approaches that reject argument from capacities altogether (§3). | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-181.md)); worth reading as the standard current survey of the grounds and weighing of animals' moral status. | [LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md) v4 | If materialism is true, the United States is probably conscious | Schwitzgebel (2014), DOI-10.1007/s11098-014-0387-8. A conditional, informal argument. Any materialist criterion liberal enough to credit rabbits (and rabbit-level distributed aliens, the "squidbits") and behaviourally human-like but oddly built aliens (Sirian supersquids, Antarean antheads) with consciousness also credits the United States. On this argument the US meets the usual materialist marks of consciousness: sophisticated information processing (roughly 10^14 person-to-person visual "connections", comparable to the brain's about 10^14 synapses), goal-directed environmental responsiveness, self-representation and historical embedding. The only exits are eliminativism, extreme sparseness or neurochauvinism, each costlier than the conclusion. The paper argues for no universal criterion. It ends undecided between three readings: US consciousness, a challenge to materialists, or grounds to distrust universal metaphysics of mind. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-131](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-131.md)); read in full (manuscript) 2026-09-26; the canonical over-generation argument against liberal materialist criteria of consciousness, and the standard critique of anti-nesting and exclusion principles, worth reading for anyone who attributes consciousness from functional or indicator properties. |

The book's thesis is that every viable theory of how consciousness fits into the cosmos, and of the cosmos's basic structure, is both "bizarre" (contrary to common sense) and "dubious" (not rationally compelling).
